Scroll through Instagram lately and you’ll probably have noticed a pattern. Accounts announcing they’re leaving. Long captions, sad goodbyes and a link to wherever they’re heading next.

And while everyone has their own reasons for going, there’s a growing sense that people have simply had enough.

Why people are fed up
For creators and small businesses, Instagram has become an increasingly frustrating place to market themselves. You spend time creating content and building an audience, only for a fraction of your followers to see what you post.

Reach fluctuates, engagement stalls, and you’re left wondering whether the problem is you or the algorithm.

Of course, not every disappointing post is Meta’s fault (we say begrudgingly). Sometimes the content simply isn’t interesting enough. But that unpredictability makes it hard for smaller businesses, with tighter budgets, to know where they stand. And now Meta has given them a few more reasons to question their investment.

What’s changed
Meta has announced Meta One, a paid subscription service gradually rolling out across Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. For businesses, the more expensive plans include clickable links in Instagram posts and Reels, advanced Story scheduling and more detailed insights.

On Facebook, the changes are a little more controversial. Some business Pages are being restricted to two organic posts or comments containing external links per month. In other words, something businesses have been doing for years could now come with a significant monthly price tag.

Meta has also proposed changes to its commercial terms that could allow it to collect content from business websites and use it to develop its own products, including AI. Following criticism and scrutiny from the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority, Meta has paused the proposals. But the fact that such changes were proposed in the first place raises questions about how much control businesses really have over their own content.

Our honest opinion
We’ll say it plainly. When a company turning over billions starts restricting features businesses have relied on for years, only to offer them back through a subscription, that isn’t innovation. It’s a toll.

We’re not against businesses paying for genuinely new and useful services. Clickable links in ordinary Instagram posts, for example, have never been widely available for free. But it’s hard to see the paywall around Facebook links as anything other than charging for something that used to be included.

What it means for agents
For most agents, nothing changes tomorrow. You can still publish posts, promote properties and have conversations with your local audience.

But if Facebook plays a part in reaching your local audience, it’s worth paying attention. Sharing a property with a link to the full listing on your website or Rightmove is standard practice for estate agents, and restricting those links on business Pages could make promoting properties considerably harder.

It’s also a reminder of something we’ve said before: don’t build your entire marketing strategy on rented land.

Your social media followers aren’t an audience you control. Meta decides how your content is distributed and which tools you have access to. That’s why building a presence beyond social media matters, whether that’s your website, your Google presence or an email database of your own.

More importantly, look beyond views and likes to what your marketing is actually achieving. Are people enquiring about properties? Are you having conversations with potential sellers? Are valuations coming from social media? Those are the results that should influence where you invest your time and money.

So, should you leave?
Our advice? Don’t make any rash decisions.

Deleting an account you’ve spent years building because of another Meta announcement probably isn’t the answer. An agent generating genuine business from Instagram has a very different decision to make from one spending hours creating content without seeing much in return.

But equally, there’s little point continuing to invest in Instagram simply because that’s what you’ve always done. If Facebook works better for your local market, give it more attention. If Google brings in valuations, invest there. If Instagram is working, keep using it.

You don’t have to like Instagram to recognise that it might still be valuable to your business. And perhaps that’s the point. Meta can change its rules whenever it likes. Your marketing strategy shouldn’t have to change with every announcement.

Instagram recently refreshed its branding for the first time in years. The changes weren't dramatic, and that's probably the point. It wasn't a completely different identity, just a more refined version of one people already recognised.

It raises an interesting question.

How do you know when it's genuinely time to refresh your branding, and when you're simply bored of looking at it?

If you run your own business, that's a surprisingly difficult question to answer.

You're not your customer

One of the challenges of running your own marketing is that you see your branding every single day.

It's on your website, your email signature, your social media, your proposals and every document you send. After a while, it's only natural to start wondering whether it needs changing.

The important thing to remember is that your customers don't experience your brand the same way you do.

They aren't looking at your logo ten times a day. They aren't comparing today's version with the one you designed three years ago. Most people simply recognise it, associate it with your business and move on.

Getting tired of your own branding isn't the same as outgrowing it.

A refresh should solve a problem

Good branding changes for a reason.

Maybe your business has evolved. Perhaps you've expanded your services, changed your audience or repositioned yourself within the market. It could simply be that the quality of your branding no longer reflects the quality of the work you're producing today.

Those are genuine reasons to refresh your identity.

Changing it because you've seen another logo you like, because you're ready for a change or because you hope a new look will generate more enquiries usually isn't.

A new logo rarely fixes a positioning problem.

Evolution beats revolution

The strongest brands rarely reinvent themselves overnight.

They evolve.

Small refinements to typography, colour, imagery or layout can make a brand feel more modern without losing the recognition you've spent years building.

That's why so many successful rebrands feel familiar. They're designed to move the brand forwards, not start again.

For most businesses, that's exactly the right approach.

Before you change anything...

If you're thinking about refreshing your branding, ask yourself one question first.

Has the business changed?

If the answer is yes, your branding may need to catch up.

If the answer is no, it might just be that you've spent a little too long looking at the same logo.

There's nothing wrong with evolving your brand. In fact, it's often a sign that your business is growing.

Just make sure you're changing it because your business needs it, not because you fancy looking at something different tomorrow morning.

One of the biggest misconceptions about social media is that you need to sit down every Monday morning and think of something completely new to post. In reality, if you’ve spent the week carrying out valuations, negotiating offers, showing buyers around homes and answering clients’ questions, you’ve probably already created enough content for the next fortnight. 


The challenge isn’t coming up with ideas, it’s recognising them.


Property posts have a place, but they can’t do all the work


Property posts have a place. They prove you’re active, showcase your instructions and give vendors confidence that you’re selling homes.


The problem is that most people following your social media aren’t looking to move today. They’re just keeping an eye on the local market, watching what sells, or quietly getting a feel for the agents in their area.


That’s why listings alone rarely build a following.


The agents who stay front of mind are usually sharing everything around the properties as well. That’s the content people come back for, the property posts simply remind them what you do.


The conversations you’re having are your content


If you’re wondering what value-add content actually looks like, you’ve probably created plenty of it already.


Think back over the last week. Maybe you’ve explained why one property sold quickly while another is still on the market, talked somebody through exchange and completion, or helped a seller decide whether to accept an offer. Every one of those conversations could have become a post.


That’s really all value-add content is. Taking the knowledge you’re already sharing every day and putting it somewhere your audience can benefit from it too.


Stop trying to reinvent the wheel


One of the biggest myths about social media is that every post has to be a brand-new idea.


It doesn’t.


Some of your best-performing content will still be just as relevant six months from now. A guide to preparing for a second viewing, an explanation of what happens after an offer is accepted or a post about the questions buyers always ask during a viewing doesn’t suddenly become irrelevant because the calendar has moved on.


The same idea can work much harder than most people realise. A question from a valuation might become a carousel, that carousel can become a talking-head video, the video can be broken into Stories, and the caption can easily be adapted into a LinkedIn post. Suddenly one conversation has become four pieces of content without needing four completely different ideas.


That’s not cutting corners. It’s simply making your content work harder.


A blank screen is usually the problem


Most agents don’t struggle because they don’t know enough. They struggle because every time they sit down to post, they’re starting from scratch wondering what to say, how it should look and whether anybody will actually engage with it.


That’s the part that drains the enthusiasm and makes consistency difficult, even for agents who genuinely enjoy creating content.


Why we built The Edit


When we started creating content for estate agents every day, we kept seeing the same themes appear again and again: market updates, educational content, community posts, personal branding and buying and selling advice. The ideas weren’t the problem. Starting from a blank page was.


That’s why we created The Edit.


Rather than expecting agents to design every post themselves, we built a growing collection of editable template packs around the types of content that consistently work in estate agency. Not generic business templates with a house dropped onto them, but professionally designed content built around the conversations your audience is already interested in.


You still add your local knowledge, your personality and your opinion. The templates simply give you the framework, so instead of spending an hour deciding how a post should look, you can spend that time sharing something genuinely useful.


Because your knowledge is what makes the content valuable.

Every estate agent has photographed a property that looked fantastic in person, only to get back to the office and wonder where all the space went.

 

The living room suddenly feels smaller. The bright kitchen looks a little flat. Somehow the house you’ve just walked around doesn’t quite feel like the one on your screen.

 

Good property photography isn’t about making a home look better than it is. It’s about making it feel the way it did when you first walked through the front door.

 

Rightmove’s own guidance to sellers highlights that photographs are usually the very first thing buyers notice when browsing listings, long before they’ve read a description or looked at the floorplan.

 

The camera isn’t usually the problem

 

One of the biggest misconceptions around property photography is that better images come from better equipment.

 

Sometimes they do.

Often they don’t.

 

We’ve seen beautifully marketed £300,000 homes photographed on an iPhone, and we’ve seen expensive homes let down by rushed images taken on cameras that cost thousands. Preparation nearly always has a bigger impact than equipment.

 

Beds made properly. Worktops cleared. Curtains open. Every light switched on. Taking a minute to move the recycling bin, straighten the dining chairs or wipe fingerprints off the patio doors before pressing the shutter.

 

The little things add up.


Buyers notice more than you think

 

One of the easiest ways to spot rushed photography is that every room has been photographed from exactly the same place, usually the doorway. Technically there’s nothing wrong with that, but it doesn’t tell a story.

 

The best property photographers aren’t simply documenting rooms. They’re guiding buyers through a home, choosing angles that highlight natural light, the flow between spaces and the features that make one property different from the next.

 

Your portal photos and your social media photos have different jobs

 

This is probably the mistake we see most often. The image that earns a click on Rightmove isn’t necessarily the image that performs best on Instagram.

 

On a property portal, buyers are comparing dozens of homes side by side. Your lead image has one job: convince somebody that this property is worth opening. 


Social media is completely different. You’re competing with family photos, local news, holidays and everything else in someone’s feed. That’s where tighter crops, interesting details and more editorial-style imagery often outperform another wide-angle photograph of the living room.

 

More isn’t always better

 

There’s a temptation to upload every photograph from the shoot. But, most buyers don’t need four angles of the same bedroom or three photographs of the downstairs WC. 


A tighter selection of genuinely good images nearly always creates a stronger listing than thirty photographs that all say the same thing. Every image should earn its place.

 

So when is professional photography worth it?

 

Not every property needs the same level of investment.

 

For plenty of entry-level homes, careful preparation and thoughtful photography on a modern smartphone will produce excellent results. We’d rather see well-executed phone photography than rushed professional photography every day of the week.

 

Budget plays a part too. The marketing budget for a £200,000 home is naturally different to the budget for a £1 million property, but the principle stays the same. The level of presentation should match both the property and the expectations of the vendor. Premium homes generally justify a premium marketing package because buyers expect it, and vendors do too.

 

Equipment and budget are easy to talk about. Skill is the part that often gets quietly ignored.

 

Owning a phone that’s capable of taking great photographs doesn’t automatically mean you’ll produce great property photography. Understanding composition, choosing the right angle, working with natural light and knowing what buyers actually need to see all take practice.

 

If photography isn’t something you’ve invested time in learning, that’s absolutely fine, but be honest with yourself. If you don’t have the time or interest to learn the craft properly, bring somebody in who does.

 

There’s no prize for doing it yourself.

 

What you’re really paying for

 

A professional photographer isn’t valuable because they own an expensive camera.

They’re valuable because they know how to present a property at its best, from planning the shot through to the final edit.

 

Before the shutter is pressed, they’re thinking about the light, the angle, the composition and the small details that most people overlook. They’ll move furniture, straighten artwork, open doors, switch lamps on and off, and take several photographs from slightly different positions before deciding which one works best.

 

Then comes the part buyers never see.

 

Professional editing isn’t about making a property look like something it isn’t. It’s about correcting perspective, balancing exposure, ensuring colours look natural and creating a consistent set of images that accurately reflect how the property felt in person. Done well, buyers shouldn’t notice the editing at all. They should simply feel that the home looks inviting and well presented.

 

Our final thought

 

Professional photography isn’t the right answer for every property.

But every property deserves good photography.


Sometimes that means a carefully planned phone shoot. Sometimes it means bringing in a specialist photographer. The important thing isn’t who presses the shutter, it’s whether the finished photographs do the property justice.


Then there’s video.


For the right property, photography and videography belong in the same conversation. A well-produced property film does something still images can’t, it captures how a home actually feels to move through. The proportion of the rooms, the way natural light changes throughout the property, and the sense of space that a photograph can only suggest.


If a property warrants investment in professional photography, it’s well worth asking whether video should be part of the same brief. More often than not, the properties that benefit from one will benefit from the other.

Most self-employed estate agents have had the same thought at some point.


You take on a property that could genuinely benefit from professional photography, a video walkthrough, some paid social advertising or a properly planned launch.


Then reality kicks in.

You’re the one paying for it.


For most instructions, that’s simply part of the process. You invest in the marketing before you’ve earned a penny, which naturally limits how much you’re able to justify spending on any one instruction. Most of the time that’s perfectly reasonable. But every now and then a property comes along where you can’t help thinking, “If I had a bigger marketing budget, I could do this one properly."


The biggest objection is usually your own


The conversation around marketing fees often starts with the assumption that vendors won’t pay for them.

In reality, many agents never actually ask.


They decide the answer will be “no” before they’ve explained what they’re proposing, because charging anything upfront feels uncomfortable in a market that’s built around “no sale, no fee”.


Not every vendor will agree to it.

But not every property needs it either.


It isn’t about the fee


The easiest way to think about a marketing fee is to stop calling it one. A vendor isn’t paying for “marketing”. They’re investing in a bespoke marketing campaign that’s designed specifically for their property, that’s an important difference.


A unique country home, an architect-designed property or a premium listing often needs more than a standard launch. Professional photography, video, targeted social advertising, premium printed material or an open house aren’t extras for the sake of it, they’re tools designed to reach the right buyer.


The recommendation should always come from the property, not from a list of services you’re trying to sell.


Present a proposal, not a price


The conversation is much easier when you explain the thinking before you explain the cost.


Talk about the likely buyer. Explain why this property deserves a different approach. Show the vendor exactly what you’d do, why you’re recommending it and how it could improve the marketing of their home.


At that point, you’re no longer asking someone to pay an additional fee.

You’re presenting a considered marketing proposal.


Some vendors will decide it’s not for them, and that’s absolutely fine. Others will see it as an investment in achieving the best possible result.


Our final thought


A marketing fee shouldn’t become the default.

Most properties don’t need one.


But if you’ve ever looked at a property and thought, “I’d market this completely differently if I had the budget,” it might be worth asking whether the conversation you’re avoiding is actually the one that could deliver the best outcome for your client.


Because sometimes the difference between standard marketing and exceptional marketing isn’t creativity.

It’s having the budget to do it properly.

The valuation used to be the start of the relationship.


A seller would decide they were considering a move, call a few local agents, book some valuations and decide from there. Reputation mattered, boards mattered, the branch mattered, and the agent who performed best in the room usually had a strong chance of winning the instruction.


That version of estate agency still exists, especially in more traditional markets. But for a lot of sellers, the journey now starts much earlier.


They might follow a local agent months before they are ready to move. They might watch the market quietly through Instagram, Facebook or TikTok, or notice which homes are selling, which agents are active and who seems to understand the area properly.


By the time they book a valuation, the relationship has already started. You just don’t know it yet.  


The journey looks different now


Social media hasn't simply given estate agents another place to advertise properties. It's changed the order in which people experience an agent.


A seller no longer needs to walk past your office window to know who you are, or what you’re listing. They can see your market updates, your sold posts, your property videos, your local commentary and your face long before they need your services.


That matters because the early part of the seller journey is often quiet. People are watching, not enquiring. They’re curious, not committed, building confidence slowly in the background before they’re ready to have a proper conversation.


For agents, that means the work starts earlier too.


Visibility does not mean what it used to


Historically, visibility in estate agency was very physical. A high-street office. Boards in the area. Printed brochures. Local newspaper adverts. The brands with the biggest presence were often the brands people remembered first.


Social media has completely redefined what visibility looks like.

Now, an independent agent can appear in someone’s feed three times a week without needing a branch on the high street or a huge advertising budget. A self-employed agent can talk directly to local sellers, share their opinion on the market and show the way they work in a way that feels much more immediate than a polished corporate campaign.


That doesn’t mean the bigger brands have lost their advantage.

It means the smaller agents have gained one. 


Social media rewards people, not logos


This is where the opportunity becomes interesting for self-employed agents and small independents.


Corporate brands are often built around consistency, control and recognition. Social media works differently. It rewards content that feels specific, timely and human, which is much easier to create when the person posting is also the person doing the valuations, meeting the sellers and walking through the homes.


A national brand might have more budget, but an independent agent can often move faster. They can film a quick market update after a valuation, share a thought from a viewing or comment on something that’s happened in their local market that morning.


That kind of content is hard to fake from a central marketing team.


The advantage only exists if you use it


Social media has made it easier for smaller agents to compete, but it hasn’t made it automatic. Showing up once a month isn’t enough. Posting only listings isn’t enough. Sharing generic content that could belong to any agent in any town isn’t enough.


The agents who benefit are the ones who are consistently visible, genuinely useful and recognisably themselves, because they understand where the seller journey begins.


The valuation used to be the start of the relationship.

Today, it’s often just the first time you’ve actually met.

I’ve bought more template packs than I should probably admit over the years.


Working in marketing, it’s part of the job. Sometimes it’s for inspiration, sometimes it’s to see how other designers approach a problem, and occasionally it’s simply because somebody’s built something really good.


The templates themselves weren’t a problem.

But the editing experience could be.


For me, opening everything in Canva isn’t a problem. I use it every day. But after working with estate agents for years, it became obvious that wasn’t everyone’s experience. We kept seeing the same thing. Great templates, but people feeling less confident once they actually came to edit them.


That’s where the idea for The Studio started.


Rather than sending people somewhere else to edit their templates, we wanted everything to live in one place. Buy a pack, open your member area, choose the design you want, edit it and download it. No searching through huge template files. No wondering whether you need the paid version. Just a straightforward editing experience designed around the people using it.


We also wanted to remove some of the frustrations that tend to slow people down. Our editing tools cover everything most estate agents need to design social media posts, your Brand Kit keeps your colours and fonts ready to go, and once you’ve bought a pack, The Studio is yours to use for your own designs too, not just the templates you’ve purchased.


The feature we’re probably proudest of isn’t a design tool at all.


It’s the support.


Instead of opening another browser tab to search for a tutorial or sending us an email, you can simply ask the built-in assistant how to do something. If you’re stuck, it walks you through it there and then, and we’re continuing to build more guides and support into the platform all the time.


The Studio was never meant to compete with professional design software.


It was built to remove the barriers that stop people creating content in the first place.


Because buying a template should be the start of the process, not the beginning of another learning curve.

Scroll through the social media pages of most local estate agents and you’ll probably notice a familiar pattern. New instruction. Price reduction. Sold STC. Completion day. Repeat.

 

And there’s nothing wrong with that... Properties need marketing, and every one of those posts has its place. The problem is that if everyone’s feed looks the same, there’s very little to remember once you’ve finished scrolling.


The agents who tend to stand out are rarely doing anything revolutionary. They’re just making themselves part of the content. They’re talking about the local market, filming the occasional walkthrough, sharing what happened at a valuation that morning or explaining why a particular property generated so much interest. Over time, people stop recognising just the agency, they start recognising the agent.

 

The valuation starts long before the appointment

One of the most common things we hear from agents is, “They said they’d been following me for a while.”

Usually, that homeowner has never liked a post, left a comment or sent a message. They’ve simply watched from a distance, seeing the occasional market update, property tour or sold story appear in their feed over a period of weeks or months.

 

By the time they enquire, they already feel like they know you.

 

That changes the conversation. You’re no longer introducing yourself from scratch, you’re walking into a valuation where the homeowner already has a sense of who you are, how you communicate and whether they trust your opinion.

 

The agents people remember aren’t always the loudest 

It’s easy to assume you need bigger videos, better editing or more elaborate content to build a personal brand.

From what we’ve seen, that’s rarely the difference.

 

The agents who build the strongest following in their area are usually the ones who show up consistently. Their videos have a familiar style, they have an opinion on what’s happening locally, and they’re comfortable appearing on camera even when the video isn’t perfect.

 

The funny thing is that homeowners rarely remember your best post. More often, they remember that they’ve seen you before.

 

Don’t let your social media become another property portal

If every post is another listing, every estate agency starts looking remarkably similar.

The content that tends to generate conversations is everything around the properties. Explaining why a home sold so quickly. Talking about pricing mistakes sellers commonly make. Sharing what buyers are asking for this month. Answering the question that came up in three valuations this week.

 

That’s the sort of content people can’t find on a property portal, and it’s often the content that positions you as the local expert rather than simply the person marketing the house.

 

Most agents aren’t avoiding personal branding, they’re avoiding the camera

Almost everyone feels awkward talking to a phone at first.

Watch yourself back and you’ll probably pick apart everything, your voice, where you were looking, what your hands were doing and whether you should have started again.

 

The reality is that your audience isn’t analysing any of that. They’re deciding whether you seem knowledgeable, approachable and like someone they’d be happy inviting into their home.

 

Those are very different things.

 

If you’re not sure where to start

Personal branding doesn’t need an elaborate content strategy.

  • Film a one-minute market update after a busy morning.
  • Record a quick walkthrough of a new instruction.
  • Talk about a question that came up during a valuation.
  • Explain why one property attracted five offers while another is still sitting on the market.

None of those ideas take long, and none require expensive equipment. They’re simply moments from your working week that demonstrate your knowledge and personality.

 

Do that consistently for a few months and something interesting starts to happen. People begin mentioning your videos during valuations. Friends tag each other in your posts. Recommendations become a little more frequent because your name is already familiar before anyone makes an enquiry.

 

That’s really what personal branding is.

Not trying to become an influencer, or chasing viral content, but making sure that when someone in your area finally decides to move, they already know who they’re going to call.

The best property video isn't always the most expensive. A confident, well-lit, steady phone walkthrough, with a real agent talking through the home, often outperforms a glossy drone production, because it feels honest and human. Here's how to shoot one that will attract the attention of a potential buyer.

Before you press record

Walk every room as if you're a buyer seeing it for the first time. You'll notice things you've stopped seeing like...

  • Beds and bedrooms. Sheets creased, pillows squashed, a dressing gown on the back of the door. Make the bed properly, pulled tight, pillows squared. Remove everything from bedside tables except a lamp and one book. Close the wardrobe.
  • Kitchen. Clear the worktops entirely. Everything. The toaster, the knife block, the fruit bowl, the pile of post. One cafetière and a plant if you want it to look lived-in. Hide the bin. Tuck away or unplug every visible cable.
  • Bathrooms. Toilet lid down, always. Remove the bathroom bin, the shampoo bottles from the shower, the soap dish if it's seen better days. A clean towel folded neatly on the rail is enough.
  • Living spaces. Straighten the cushions, remove the throws if they're crumpled, hide the remote controls. If there's a fireplace, make it a feature, clear the hearth and light it if it's winter.
  • The details that kill footage. A charging cable across the kitchen counter. A recycling bag by the back door. A child's drawing half-stuck to the fridge. These things disappear in person but dominate on camera.

One final check before you start: open every curtain, turn on every light, and wipe the lens. A smudged lens is the single most common reason phone footage looks foggy, and it takes ten seconds to fix.

Shooting technique

Hold the phone in both hands, elbows tucked into your body for stability, and walk heel-to-toe, slowly, like you're carrying a full cup of coffee. Move the camera deliberately - slow pans, no whip-arounds. Film in landscape for the website and portrait for social; if in doubt, shoot a vertical pass for reels and a horizontal pass for the listing.

Slow and steady reads as premium. Fast and shaky reads as amateur, even in a beautiful home.

A note on audio

Nobody talks about audio in phone walkthroughs. They should.

Bad audio is the fastest way to make otherwise good footage feel amateur. Before you start, stand still and listen. Is the boiler about to fire? Is there a window open onto a busy road? Is the extractor fan still running from when you turned the kitchen light on?

Phone microphones are surprisingly good in quiet conditions and surprisingly bad in anything else. Wind is the biggest culprit outdoors, even a gentle breeze makes exterior shots unusable. If you're filming outside, shield the mic with your hand or body and keep clips short.

For agent-led walkthroughs, speak clearly and at a normal pace. The temptation is to rush. The footage always sounds faster than it felt. If a take has a noticeable noise in the background — a car, a door, someone's phone — do it again. It takes thirty seconds and it's always worth it.

The agent-led walkthrough

The version that builds your brand as well as selling the house is the one with you in it. Walk and talk: "Through here is the kitchen, and this is the bit everyone falls for." It's harder, it takes a couple of takes, and it's worth it. A face and a voice turn a property tour into a piece of personal-brand content that works long after the house is sold.

A simple, repeatable routine

  • Natural light, lens wiped, both hands, slow heel-to-toe, best feature last, one vertical pass and one horizontal.
  • Edit your content in CapCut and add captions if there's audio.
  • Keep it under sixty seconds for social.

Do it on every instruction and within a month you'll have a body of work, and a noticeably stronger feed, for the price of fifteen extra minutes per viewing.

A well-filmed phone walkthrough, prepared properly and shot with care, will outperform a rushed professional production every time. For most instructions, it's exactly the right tool. But for the properties that deserve more — the ones where the light, the space, and the story of the home need to be captured properly — a professional shoot changes what's possible. Worth knowing the difference before you press record.
